Check missing values, and what they imply for complete cases

Source: R/ilm_missing.R, R/zzz-iml-aliases.R
ilm_check_missing.Rd

ilm_check_missing() reports how much of a data frame is missing, which variables go missing together, what missingness is associated with among the observed values, and, when an outcome y is named, whether missingness depends on the outcome once the covariates are held fixed. It then states what that implies for a complete-case analysis of a regression of y on the covariates.

Usage

ilm_check_missing(
  data,
  y = NULL,
  covariates = NULL,
  min_effect = 0.1,
  alpha = 0.05,
  adjust = "holm",
  verbose = TRUE,
  unit = NULL,
  covariates_negate = FALSE,
  covariates_fixed = FALSE,
  subset = NULL,
  subset_negate = FALSE,
  subset_fixed = FALSE
)

# S3 method for class 'ilm_missing'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

data

A data frame.

y

Optional outcome: a single string naming a column, or a formula outcome ~ predictors. With a formula, the response becomes y and the variables on the right-hand side become covariates, exactly as if they had been given by name; an explicit covariates takes precedence. A right-hand side of . means every other column.

covariates

The columns held fixed in the outcome test, in any of the forms described in ilm_selection. NULL (the default) means every column except y and unit.

min_effect

The smallest effect that counts as a finding, in the screen and in the outcome test (default 0.1). An illumex choice.

alpha

The level for the adjusted p-values (default 0.05).

adjust

The multiplicity method: any method that stats::p.adjust() accepts (default "holm"). The screen's p-values are adjusted across all of its rows; the outcome test's across its rows.

verbose

If TRUE (the default), narrate the findings as messages.

unit

Optional: a single string naming the column that identifies the unit (subject, household) when the data have several rows per unit. It may not be y or one of the named covariates, and it may not have missing values. See "Several rows per unit".

covariates_negate, covariates_fixed

How covariates is read, as described in ilm_selection. covariates_negate = TRUE keeps every column except those that covariates selects, and so needs covariates. covariates_fixed = TRUE matches a pattern in covariates literally rather than as a regular expression.

subset

Which rows to use, before anything else: a logical vector (one value per row; NA is left out), row positions, named patterns (c(site = "^north")), or ilm_sample(). See ilm_selection. Results keep the data's own row numbers.

subset_negate

If TRUE, the rows subset would not take: the other rows, or the rows not sampled (a holdout). With a logical subset, rows where it is NA stay out either way.

subset_fixed

If TRUE, subset's patterns are matched literally, as substrings. It changes nothing for a logical, positions or a sample.

x

An ilm_missing object.

...

Not used.

Value

An object of class "ilm_missing": a list with these fields, in this order.

  • variables: a data frame with one row per column (after subset): variable, n_missing (an integer) and p_missing (the share missing), largest share first.

  • patterns: NULL when nothing is missing; otherwise a data frame with pattern (a string of 0s and 1s, one character per column with missing values, in the data's order, 1 where that column is missing), n (the rows with that pattern) and n_missing (the number of 1s), most common first. Its attribute "variables" names those columns.

  • associations: the association screen, or NULL when no pair qualifies (and when nothing is missing). Columns missing_in, related_to, effect, p_value, is_outcome (related_to is y), p_adj, flag and method; largest effect first.

  • outcome_test: NULL when y is not named or nothing is missing; otherwise one row per column with missing values, in the data's order: missing_in, effect, p_value, p_adj, flag and method.

  • monotone: TRUE or FALSE; NA when nothing is missing.

  • n: the number of rows after subset (an integer).

  • n_complete: the number of rows with no missing value (an integer).

  • y: the outcome's name, or NULL.

  • min_effect: as given.

  • unit: the unit column's name, or NULL.

  • n_units: the number of distinct units after subset (an integer); NA without unit.

  • verdict: "NONE", "RELATED_TO_OUTCOME", "RELATED_TO_COVARIATES" or "MCAR_NOT_REJECTED".

Details

How much, and where. variables gives each column's missing count and share. patterns tabulates the rows' patterns of missingness over the columns that have any missing value. monotone says whether those columns can be ordered so that each is missing wherever the one before it is missing (Little and Rubin 2019, p. 11). The check orders the columns by their missing counts, smallest first, and compares neighbours.

The association screen. For each column v with missing values and each other column w, the indicator "v is missing" is compared across the values of w, over the rows where w is observed.

  • A numeric w (integer or double) gives the absolute Pearson correlation between the indicator and w, with the usual two-sided t test on n - 2 degrees of freedom.

  • Any other w (logical, character, factor, Date, date-time or duration; one level per distinct value) is cross-tabulated against the indicator. The p-value is Pearson's chi-squared test of independence without a continuity correction, and the effect is Cramér's V (Agresti 2013, p. 110).

  • A pair is skipped when fewer than 10 rows remain, when the indicator takes one value there, or when w has no spread (or fewer than two levels).

  • The p-values are adjusted across all pairs by adjust. A pair is flagged when its adjusted p-value is below alpha AND its effect is at least min_effect: with many rows, a negligible association is significant.

A correlation and a Cramér's V are not the same quantity; they are sorted together on one 0-1 scale for convenience. The screen describes; a flag on the outcome column does not by itself mean that complete cases are biased (see "Why 'not MCAR' does not mean 'impute'").

The outcome test (only when y is named). For each column v with missing values, over the rows with y and the covariates observed, two logistic regressions of "v is missing" are fitted, each with an intercept: one on the covariates, one on the covariates plus y. Numeric covariates enter linearly, categorical ones (factor, character, logical) as treatment-coded indicators. A numeric y enters as one column; a categorical y, with k levels present, as k - 1 indicators.

  • A Date, date-time (POSIXct) or duration (difftime) covariate, or y, is judged as a numeric one is: it is left out only when it has no spread on the rows used. It enters both regressions, and the effect's least-squares step, as ONE numeric column, its numeric value (days for a Date, seconds for a date-time, the stored number for a duration) counted from its earliest value on those rows, whatever its number of distinct values: a daily date is kept, as a linear time term. For a linear term with an intercept, neither the unit nor the starting point changes the test or the effect. In the screen such columns stay categorical.

  • The p-value is the likelihood-ratio test between the two fits.

  • The effect is the multiple correlation between the Pearson residuals of the covariates-only fit and y's model columns, each residualised on the covariates by least squares. For a numeric, date or two-level y this is the absolute partial correlation ("partial r"); for a y with more levels it is a multiple partial correlation ("partial R"). It does not depend on which level is the reference, or on the order of the levels. It measures the association given the covariates, because bias depends on that conditional association, not on the marginal one.

  • Covariates with no spread, with fewer than two levels, or with more than 20 levels are left out of the models.

  • Fewer than 20 rows, an indicator that takes one value, or a failed fit give NA. Missingness in y itself gives NA (see below).

  • The covariates are covariates without v and y; when covariates is not given, every column except y, v and unit.

The verdict, in order of precedence: "NONE" (nothing is missing); "RELATED_TO_OUTCOME" (an outcome-test row is flagged); "RELATED_TO_COVARIATES" (a screen row is flagged); otherwise "MCAR_NOT_REJECTED".

What can and cannot be established

Missingness completely at random (MCAR) can be REJECTED by the screen, never confirmed. A screen that flags nothing is consistent with MCAR, but such tests have limited power when few units are incomplete (Little and Rubin 2019, section 3.2, p. 50). The verdict "MCAR_NOT_REJECTED" says that and no more.

Whether missingness depends on the unseen values themselves (missing at random against missing not at random: MAR against MNAR) cannot be tested from the observed data. Such comparisons give "no direct evidence" on MAR (Little and Rubin 2019, p. 50), and there can be no evidence against MAR in the observed data (Little and Rubin 2019, Example 13.2, p. 306). Every verdict except "NONE" therefore ends with this caveat, and recommends a sensitivity analysis to assess departures from MAR.

The outcome test has a limit of its own. When a covariate goes missing because of its OWN unseen values (for example, a covariate missing more often when it is large), complete cases are still unbiased: Little and Rubin (2019, Example 3.3, p. 49) include such mechanisms among the unbiased ones, as do Hughes et al. (2019, Table 1, p. 1297, row "Exposure"). The outcome test cannot hold that covariate's unseen values fixed, so the outcome carries information about them, and the test can flag the outcome there although complete cases are unbiased. That is this package's own finding about its own test, shown by simulation. So "RELATED_TO_OUTCOME" means that complete-case estimates MAY be biased, never that they are.

Why 'not MCAR' does not mean 'impute'

Complete-case analysis of a regression of y on covariates X is unbiased when the chance of being a complete case is independent of y given X, even when it depends strongly on X (White and Carlin 2010, section 2.2, p. 2921; Hughes et al. 2019, p. 1296 and Table 1, p. 1297; Little and Rubin 2019, Example 3.3, p. 49). That condition is weaker than MCAR, and it cuts across MCAR, MAR and MNAR. X includes the incomplete covariate's own values: the condition can hold when a covariate's missingness depends on its own missing values (White and Carlin 2010, section 2.2, p. 2921; Little and Rubin 2019, Example 3.3, p. 49, which includes such mechanisms).

Each verdict's message gives the number of missing values and the number of columns that have them, so that the weight of the evidence can be judged.

When nothing is flagged ("MCAR_NOT_REJECTED"), there is no evidence that missingness is related to any observed variable. Such checks are useful, but they have limited power when the incomplete units are few (Little and Rubin 2019, section 3.2, p. 50): "not rejected" is not evidence of absence.

When missingness is related to the covariates, with no evidence of a relation to the outcome given them ("RELATED_TO_COVARIATES"), complete cases stay unbiased for the regression on those covariates, unless missingness depends on unseen values. That holds whenever being complete is independent of y given the covariates, the incomplete covariate's own values included (White and Carlin 2010, section 2.2, p. 2921; Little and Rubin 2019, Example 3.3, p. 49). Imputation is not needed for correctness, though it can recover precision. This function distinguishes that case and says so, rather than sending you to imputation.

When missingness is related to the outcome given the covariates ("RELATED_TO_OUTCOME"), complete-case estimates MAY be biased.

  • Not when a covariate is missing because of its own value. Complete cases are unbiased when missingness depends on the covariate, including the missing-not-at-random mechanism p(C | X, Y) = f(X), where C is being complete (White and Carlin 2010, p. 2921). With one incomplete covariate, multiple imputation is valid if missingness depends on y only, complete cases if it depends on the covariate only, and both only under MCAR (White and Carlin 2010, p. 2922). When missingness is independent of the outcome given the covariates, as it is there, multiple imputation is biased away from the null (White and Carlin 2010, abstract, p. 2920): imputation assuming MAR is the biased choice. The outcome test can flag this case (see "What can and cannot be established").

  • Nor in the cases of Hughes et al. (2019, Table 1, p. 1297, and p. 1298): a linear regression whose true coefficient is zero; and the exposure odds ratio of a logistic regression when completeness depends on the outcome alone, on the outcome and the confounders, or on the outcome and the exposure independently. That logistic exception does not apply when the binary outcome dichotomises a continuous one on which missingness depends (Hughes et al. 2019, p. 1298).

Multiple imputation (illume::ilm_impute(), then illume::ilm_mi_pool()) is the analysis under MAR. It is often preferred when auxiliary variables make MAR more plausible (Hughes et al. 2019, p. 1302; White and Carlin 2010, p. 2928). Run the complete-case analysis as well: "It is, however, valuable to perform both MI and CC analyses ... Any differences should be explained" (White and Carlin 2010, p. 2928). Choosing between the two by their standard errors is misleading (White and Carlin 2010, abstract, p. 2920, and p. 2928).

When y itself has missing values, its own row of the outcome test is NA: rows missing y leave the analysis, so the indicator is constant there. With missing outcome only, complete cases are unbiased exactly when the outcome is MAR given the covariates (White and Carlin 2010, p. 2921), and whether the outcome's missingness depends on its own unseen values cannot be tested (Little and Rubin 2019, p. 50).

Several rows per unit

The sources assume independent rows (Little and Rubin 2019, p. 13). With several rows per unit (a subject seen at several visits, the members of a household), every p-value computed as if the rows were independent is too small. Name the column that identifies the unit in unit. Each test is then run in one of two ways.

  • One row per unit, when, over the rows the test uses, every unit has a single value of the missingness indicator AND a single value of each variable the test uses (w for the screen; y and the covariates for the outcome test). Each unit's first such row is kept, and the test runs exactly as above with units in place of rows; the 10- and 20-row floors count units. The test's variables must be constant too, not only missingness, because a variable that varies within a unit has no single value to keep.

  • Otherwise, a cluster-robust test. The logistic regression is fitted by ordinary maximum likelihood on the rows, its covariance is estimated by the sandwich with the scores summed within units (Liang and Zeger 1986), and the tested coefficients (of w, or of y) get a Wald test. With fewer than 30 units among the rows the test uses, the p-value is NA. No small-sample correction is applied. Standard errors from the sandwich tend to be too small in finite samples (Firth 1993, p. 344), and with few units they tend to underestimate the true ones (Agresti 2013, p. 468), so the test can reject too often. illumex's own size study measured this for this function, at alpha = 0.05 over 2,000 simulated data sets per setting: with 5 rows in every unit, the rejection rate was 0.08 to 0.09 at 20 and 25 units, and between 0.05 and 0.07 from 30 units up, within the band of 0.025 to 0.075 that Bradley (1978, p. 146) calls liberal; with between 2 and 8 rows per unit, it was 0.08 to 0.10 at 20 and at 30 units, above that band. Treat a p-value near alpha with caution when units are few, or when their sizes differ.

On the cluster-robust route, effects are computed on the rows as described above; on the one-row-per-unit route, on the units. The method column of associations and outcome_test says how each test ran: "rows" (no unit), "units" (one row per unit) or "sandwich". The unit column is left out of the screen, the covariates, the patterns and the monotone check; it still appears in variables.

When unit is NULL and the data look like several rows per unit, a warning says that the p-values assume independent rows and suggests unit. It is given at most once per call, even with verbose = FALSE, and it never changes the result. The check behind it finds a grouping only in a categorical column, so a numeric identifier column is not detected: name unit whenever the data have several rows per unit.

What is published and what is this package's own

Published: the condition under which complete cases are unbiased (White and Carlin 2010, p. 2921; Hughes et al. 2019, pp. 1296-1298; Little and Rubin 2019, p. 49); comparing the complete with the incomplete units to judge MCAR, and the limits of doing so (Little and Rubin 2019, p. 50); the definition of a monotone pattern (Little and Rubin 2019, p. 11); Cramér's V, the square root of Cramér's measure of association X^2 / (n (q - 1)), q the smaller of the table's numbers of rows and columns (Cramér 1946, section 30.5, p. 443; Agresti 2013, p. 110); and the sandwich variance of the independence working model (Liang and Zeger 1986, pp. 14-15; Agresti 2013, pp. 467-469).

illumex's own operationalisations, which no source prescribes: the association screen's per-variable form (it compares by each variable's own missingness indicator, a variant of Little and Rubin's comparison of complete with incomplete units); its effect measures, and sorting them on one scale; the thresholds (min_effect, the 10- and 20-row floors, the 30-unit floor, the 20-level cut-off) and the defaults of alpha and adjust; the multiplicity rule and the requirement of both significance and size for a flag; the way monotonicity is checked; the outcome test and its effect measure; the treatment of Date, date-time and duration columns (categorical in the screen; one numeric column in the outcome test, whatever their number of distinct values); the verdict labels, their precedence and the wording of their messages; the rule choosing between one row per unit and the sandwich; and the Wald test of several coefficients at once.

References

Agresti, A. (2013). Categorical Data Analysis, 3rd ed. Wiley.

Bradley, J. V. (1978). Robustness? British Journal of Mathematical and Statistical Psychology 31, 144-152.

Cramér, H. (1946). Mathematical Methods of Statistics. Princeton University Press.

Firth, D. (1993). Recent developments in quasi-likelihood methods. Bulletin of the International Statistical Institute 55, 341-358.

Hughes, R. A., Heron, J., Sterne, J. A. C. and Tilling, K. (2019). Accounting for missing data in statistical analyses: multiple imputation is not always the answer. International Journal of Epidemiology 48(4), 1294-1304.

Liang, K.-Y. and Zeger, S. L. (1986). Longitudinal data analysis using generalized linear models. Biometrika 73, 13-22.

Little, R. J. A. and Rubin, D. B. (2019). Statistical Analysis with Missing Data, 3rd ed. Wiley.

White, I. R. and Carlin, J. B. (2010). Bias and efficiency of multiple imputation compared with complete-case analysis for missing covariate values. Statistics in Medicine 29, 2920-2931.

See also

illume::ilm_impute(), ilm_describe_na_all(), ilm_plot_missing()

Examples

d <- ilm_example_data()
ilm_check_missing(d, y = "score", verbose = FALSE)
#> <ilm_missing> 792 of 900 rows complete (88.0%)
#>   missing values:
#>     lab_value: 108 (12.0%)
#>   pattern: monotone, 2 distinct patterns
#>   verdict: MCAR_NOT_REJECTED
#>     no evidence that missingness is related to any observed variable (108 missing values in 1 column; with few missing values such checks have little power); complete cases are unbiased unless missingness depends on unseen values
#>   outcome test (missingness against `score`, given the covariates):
#>     lab_value: partial r = 0.029, adjusted p = 0.44
#>   not testable: whether missingness depends on the unseen values themselves (MNAR); no test of the observed data can rule it out, so assess it with a sensitivity analysis

# A formula names the outcome and the covariates at once
ilm_check_missing(d, score ~ income + grp, verbose = FALSE)
#> Columns: 2 of 13 (excluded: id, date, site, flag, consented, score, visits, claims, and 3 more)
#> <ilm_missing> 792 of 900 rows complete (88.0%)
#>   missing values:
#>     lab_value: 108 (12.0%)
#>   pattern: monotone, 2 distinct patterns
#>   verdict: MCAR_NOT_REJECTED
#>     no evidence that missingness is related to any observed variable (108 missing values in 1 column; with few missing values such checks have little power); complete cases are unbiased unless missingness depends on unseen values
#>   outcome test (missingness against `score`, given the covariates):
#>     lab_value: partial r = 0.033, adjusted p = 0.35
#>   not testable: whether missingness depends on the unseen values themselves (MNAR); no test of the observed data can rule it out, so assess it with a sensitivity analysis

# `id` identifies the unit: several rows per unit
ilm_check_missing(d, y = "score", unit = "id", verbose = FALSE)
#> <ilm_missing> 792 of 900 rows complete (88.0%)
#>   75 units, identified by column `id`
#>   missing values:
#>     lab_value: 108 (12.0%)
#>   pattern: monotone, 2 distinct patterns
#>   verdict: MCAR_NOT_REJECTED
#>     no evidence that missingness is related to any observed variable (108 missing values in 1 column; with few missing values such checks have little power); complete cases are unbiased unless missingness depends on unseen values
#>   outcome test (missingness against `score`, given the covariates):
#>     lab_value: partial r = 0.028, adjusted p = NA [sandwich]
#>   not testable: whether missingness depends on the unseen values themselves (MNAR); no test of the observed data can rule it out, so assess it with a sensitivity analysis
